# The Log Source

Listing 7-4 shows an example of a log source.

Listing 7-4: syslog-ng Configuration for iptables — Source

```
source src {
# include internal syslog-ng messages
# note: the internal() source is required!
#
internal();
#
# the following line will be replaced by the
# socket list generated by SuConfig using
# variables from /etc/sysconfig/syslog:
#nunix-dgram("/dev/log/")
unix-dgram("/var/lib/ntp/dev/log/")

#
# uncomment to process log messages from network:
#udp("0.0.0.0") port(514);
}
```

Listing 7-4 shows suggested definition for the syslog-ng process. This example shows two sources, /dev/log (for the standard kernel logging device) and /var/lib/ntp/dev/log. A separate entry is necessary because the NTP service runs in a jail its log source has to reside under that jail so that the npc can access it.

This example also shows a UDP entry that SUSE has commented out. This is a logging source for a network port. This is how you can set up a central logging server for your organization. By setting a source to UDP on port 514, you are enabling your machine to accept messages for logging from remote hosts. TCP/IP port 514 on UDP is the standard port for syslog messages. If you uncomment this entry, you are able to receive messages from remote hosts.

For more information on TCP/IP and specifying addresses and ports in Linux, see Chapters 6 and 15.
